partners.mechanism_chain: MMAB (HGNC:7378) —DISRUPTS→ methylmalonyl-CoA (CHEBI:16644); MMUT (HGNC:7379) —DISRUPTS→ methylmalonyl-CoA (CHEBI:16644); methylmalonyl-CoA (CHEBI:16644) —DISRUPTS→ propionate metabolism (REACT:SMR000002); propionate metabolism (REACT:SMR000002) —LEADS_TO→ methylmalonic aciduria (HP:0001874); propionate metabolism (REACT:SMR000002) —LEADS_TO→ developmental delay (HP:0001263); propionate metabolism (REACT:SMR000002) —LEADS_TO→ vomiting (HP:0011344); propionate metabolism (REACT:SMR000002) —LEADS_TO→ lethargy (HP:0011340). raw.translational: Understanding this mechanistic overlap highlights the critical role of the propionate metabolism pathway and the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase enzyme complex in preventing severe metabolic derangements and neurological damage. It suggests that therapeutic strategies targeting the downstream consequences of methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation, or potentially enhancing the function of the remaining pathway capacity, could be beneficial for both forms of methylmalonic aciduria.

raw.translational: Understanding the shared cobalamin-dependent metabolic pathway affected in both diseases can inform therapeutic strategies. Patients with cblB and cblD types may benefit from cobalamin supplementation, although the efficacy varies. Identifying specific defects in cobalamin processing or enzyme function can guide personalized treatment approaches, such as betaine for hyperhomocysteinemia.

partners.diseaseBName: methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria type cblC
partners.mechanism_chain: MMAB (HGNC:7574) —DISRUPTS→ Cobalamin metabolism (GO:0006730); Cobalamin metabolism (GO:0006730) —DECREASES→ Methylmalonyl-CoA (CHEBI:30128); Methylmalonyl-CoA (CHEBI:30128) —INCREASES→ Methylmalonic acid (CHEBI:17341); Methylmalonic acid (CHEBI:17341) —LEADS_TO→ Methylmalonic aciduria (HP:0002221); MMACHC (HGNC:7575) —DISRUPTS→ Cobalamin metabolism (GO:0006730); Cobalamin metabolism (GO:0006730) —INCREASES→ Homocysteine (CHEBI:17668); Homocysteine (CHEBI:17668) —LEADS_TO→ Homocystinuria (HP:0002137). Mutations in MMAB (cblB) and MMACHC (cblC) both impair the function of the cobalamin pathway. MMAB is required for the activity of the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Loss of MMAB function leads to methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation, which is then de-carboxylated to methylmalonic acid. MMACHC is involved in the intracellular processing and delivery of the activated cobalamin cofactor (adenosylcobalamin) to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase. Defects in MMACHC can lead to reduced activity of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (and thus methylmalonic acid accumulation) as well as methionine synthase (leading to homocysteine accumulation).

raw.translational: Understanding the shared role of cobalamin metabolism in these distinct clinical presentations can inform therapeutic strategies. While vitamin B12 supplementation is beneficial in some cobalamin-related disorders, the specific cofactor deficiencies in cblB and cblC (adenosylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin/methylcobalamin, respectively) and the resulting metabolic blockages necessitate targeted interventions. Identifying residual enzyme activity or alternative metabolic bypasses could lead to improved patient outcomes.
